transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hello, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Um, what brings me in... well, I guess what finally made me make the appointment is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach out for people has just... gone very quiet. Which is difficult, because I'm a social worker, so reaching out is kind of my whole job. I work mostly with substance abuse cases. 

Actually, they just moved my office to the second floor of our building last month, and the window looks right out onto this massive oak tree. It's a beautiful tree, really, but the glare on my computer screen around 3 PM is just awful. I had to ask maintenance for blinds three times before they finally came up, and even then, the guy who installed them tracked mud all over the carpet. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. The quietness. It's not just with people. I used to take so much pleasure in my work, and my yoga classes, going to art galleries on the weekends, even just my journaling at night. And now... I don't know, it's all just faded out. I feel like I’m mostly just moving through obligations, you know? Just waking up and doing what I'm supposed to do. I haven't even opened my journal in weeks. I used to buy these specific ones from a little shop downtown with thick, unlined paper because I like to use fountain pens, but I think that shop might have closed down during the pandemic anyway...
How long have you been experiencing this loss of interest in things you used to enjoy and this feeling of just going through the motions?

Um, let's see... I think it's been about eight months? Yeah, this whole change in how I'm thinking and working, and just... connecting with people... it really started around eight months ago. That's when we took my older relative into our apartment. 

Which, honestly, was a huge adjustment just logistically. We live in this two-bedroom place, and the second bedroom was actually my home office. I had just painted it this really calming sage green—'Quiet Willow,' I think the color was called. I bought the paint at that local hardware store down the street, the one that always has those rescue cats sleeping on the bags of potting soil near the entrance. I love going in there just to pet them, they have a little orange tabby right now that is just so sweet. 

But anyway, we had to move all my office stuff out into the living room to make space, and getting her heavy antique dresser up the stairs because it wouldn't fit in the elevator... it was just a nightmare. The building manager didn't even hold the door for the movers. 

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh. Right. Yeah, so it's been about eight months since all of this started.
Over these past 8 months, has your mood and these feelings of emptiness been pretty much constant the whole time, or have there been periods where you felt better or more like yourself?

Um, constant? I mean, I guess it's been pretty steady. I don't really remember feeling like myself at all since she moved in. It's just been this flat... gray feeling. 

Speaking of gray, I actually tried to buy a new sweater last week because the office gets so cold now that I'm near that window. I went to this little boutique near the grocery store, and they had this beautiful charcoal cashmere cardigan. But the price tag was just ridiculous. I mean, who pays that much for a sweater? And the sales clerk was so pushy, she kept trying to show me these bright red scarves that completely clashed with my skin tone. I used to wear a lot of red in my twenties, but I think it just washes me out now. 

But, um... yeah, no, I haven't really had any days where I felt better. It's just been the same quiet, empty feeling the whole time.
During these 8 months, have there been any periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep than normal, or felt unusually good or upbeat - even if just for a few days?

Um, energetic? No, not really. I don't think I've had any days like that. I've actually been sleeping pretty much the same amount, maybe even a little more, but I never wake up feeling refreshed anyway. 

It's funny you mention sleep, though, because my husband bought this new mattress pad last week. He said it was supposed to have this cooling gel technology because he always gets too hot at night. But honestly, it just feels like sleeping on a giant ice pack. I had to pull out the heavy quilt my grandmother made me just to stay warm. She knitted it entirely by hand, it took her almost two years. It's this beautiful patchwork pattern with all these little embroidered flowers in the corners. She was always so good at things like that, needlepoint, cross-stitch... I tried to learn once when I was in grad school, but I just didn't have the patience for it. I kept pricking my fingers on the needles. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right. Feeling upbeat. No, I haven't felt unusually good or energetic or anything like that. Just the same flat feeling.

I want to make sure I'm not missing anything. Over these 8 months, have there been any stretches of time—even just a week or so—where you felt more hopeful, more motivated to do things, or where you were able to get by on much less sleep than usual and still feel okay?

Um, motivated? No... I haven't really had any weeks where I felt suddenly hopeful or driven. Just finding the motivation to do basic things is so hard right now. 

Like, the other day I was trying to get motivated just to finish up my client notes for the week. We use this new electronic system at the clinic now, and administration swore it would be so much faster, but the layout is just completely awful. It's full of these tiny drop-down menus that always glitch out and freeze the screen. My coworker, Diane, she was on hold with IT for almost an hour on Tuesday trying to get her password reset. Diane's the one who always brings those little lemon scones to our morning case reviews. She says her secret is using real lemon zest instead of that bottled extract stuff. I actually tried to make them once for a potluck, but I think my oven at home runs way too hot because the bottoms completely burned. We've been meaning to call a repair guy for that oven since, gosh, maybe last Thanksgiving? The turkey cooked in half the time it was supposed to, which was nice I guess, but it dried out the white meat terribly... 

But, um... wait. Did you ask about sleep? Right, sorry. No, I haven't had any times where I needed less sleep or felt unusually good. Just the same as it's been.
Before these past 8 months, have you ever experienced a period of several weeks or longer where you felt this same kind of depression, emptiness, or loss of interest in things?

Um, before the last eight months? No, I don't... I don't think I've ever felt this empty for this long before. I mean, sure, everyone gets down sometimes, but nothing like this stretch. 

I did have a really rough patch back when I was finishing up my master's degree, though. The coursework was just so intense, and my practicum supervisor was this incredibly demanding woman. She insisted we use this very specific type of blue ink for all our physical charts. It was impossible to find! I remember driving to three different office supply stores in the pouring rain just to find these specific blue pens. And of course, the third store was out of them too, but the cashier there, he felt so bad for me he actually gave me one from his own pocket. He had this really interesting accent, I think he said he was from somewhere in Eastern Europe, maybe Poland? My husband's grandfather immigrated from Poland back in the twenties. He used to make the most amazing pierogies from scratch. He'd spend all day Sunday in the kitchen covered in flour, just pinching the edges of the dough perfectly... 

But, um... no. To answer your question, I haven't ever had a depression like this before. This is the first time it's been this bad.

When you were going through that rough patch during your master's degree, how long did that difficult period last, and how similar was it to what you're experiencing now in terms of the depth of the emptiness and loss of interest?

Um, how long did it last? I think... maybe just a few weeks? It wasn't nearly as bad as this, though. I mean, I was stressed and exhausted, but I didn't feel this complete emptiness. I still cared about things. 

I remember I was still really involved in my book club back then. We were reading this massive historical fiction novel about the French Revolution. It was over eight hundred pages long, and the author spent entire chapters just describing the architecture of Paris. I actually got to visit Paris once, right after I graduated. My husband and I went for our honeymoon. We stayed in this tiny little hotel in the Latin Quarter, and the elevator was so small we had to take our suitcases up one at a time. The concierge was this older gentleman who always wore a perfectly pressed suit, even at two in the morning. He recommended this little bistro down the street where they made the most incredible duck confit. I tried to recreate it at home once for our anniversary, but duck is just so tricky to cook right. You have to render the fat so slowly, otherwise the meat gets completely tough. I ended up having to order a pizza that night because the duck was practically inedible. The pizza delivery guy got lost because our street sign had blown down in a storm a few days before...

Wait, sorry. What did you ask me? Oh, the rough patch during grad school. Yeah, it wasn't like this. It was just stress, really. Not this... this total lack of interest in everything.

Other than that stressful period during graduate school, have you ever had another time in your life—even going back to childhood or adolescence—when you felt depressed, down, or lost interest in things you normally enjoyed for at least a couple of weeks or more?

Um, besides grad school? No, not really. I mean, I've always been pretty steady. My mom used to say I was the even-keeled one of the family. My sister, on the other hand, she was always all over the place. She went through this phase in high school where she would only wear vintage clothes from the 1970s. She found this amazing suede fringe jacket at a thrift store, but it smelled so strongly of mothballs that my mom made her hang it in the garage for a month. The garage was always so full of junk anyway. My dad had this old MG convertible that he swore he was going to restore, but it just sat there collecting dust. He bought all these specialized tools for it, and they just rusted in the toolbox. I actually still have one of those wrenches. I use it sometimes when the radiator in my office acts up. It clanks so loudly in the winter, especially during my afternoon sessions. 

But, um... no, to answer your question, I haven't ever had a time where I felt depressed or down like this for weeks at a time. Just that stress in grad school, really.

I want to ask about your energy and activity level more carefully. In these past 8 months, have there been any times—even just a few days—where you felt like you were doing MORE than usual, accomplishing more, or felt like you had more energy and drive, even if you wouldn't describe it as feeling 'good'?

Um, more energy? No... no, I haven't had any days where I felt like I was doing more than usual. Honestly, getting out of bed has been the biggest accomplishment lately. 

I used to have so much energy, though. When I first started at the clinic, I was running two therapy groups a week on top of my individual caseload. We had this one group room, room B, and the chairs in there were those awful molded plastic ones from the nineties. They were this bright, obnoxious teal color. I tried for months to get the clinic director to approve a budget for new chairs. He was this very stern man who always drank his coffee out of a travel mug that looked like a camera lens. It was actually a really clever design, my nephew has one just like it. He's really into photography, mostly black and white landscapes. He took this incredible photo of a lone pine tree up in the mountains last winter. He printed it on this special textured paper and framed it for my birthday. I hung it right above the fireplace, but then the hook gave out a few weeks ago and it fell. Thankfully the glass didn't break, but it chipped the mantle... 

Sorry, I lost my train of thought. But no, I haven't felt any extra energy or drive or anything like that in the last eight months. Just... just the opposite, really.

In the year or two before these 8 months started—so roughly from two to three years ago until about 8 months ago—did you notice any periods where your mood felt lower, even if it wasn't as severe as what you're experiencing now?

Um, in the year or two before all this started? No, I don't think so. I felt pretty normal back then. My mood was fine. 

That was around the time we finally decided to redo the kitchen, actually. We had these awful linoleum floors that were peeling up at the corners, and the cabinets were this really dark, depressing oak. We ended up going with a light gray for the cabinets, which really brightened the place up. The contractor we hired, his name was Dave, he was always bringing his golden retriever to the house while he worked. The dog's name was Buster, and he was the sweetest thing, but he shed everywhere. I was constantly vacuuming up dog hair, even after Dave left for the day. My husband bought one of those robot vacuums to help out, you know, the ones that just wander around the house on their own? It worked okay for a while, but then it got stuck under the sofa and just kept beeping until the battery died. I had to get down on my hands and knees with a broom handle to fish it out. It was covered in dust bunnies. I think we ended up giving it to my neighbor's daughter when she moved into her first apartment. She was so excited about it, she sent us a thank you card with a picture of her cat sitting on top of it...

But, wait. What were we talking about? Oh, my mood before all this. Yeah, no, I felt fine. I wasn't feeling low or anything like that. Just regular, you know?

The garage was always so full of junk anyway. My dad had this old MG convertible that he swore he was going to restore, but it just sat there collecting dust. He bought all these specialized tools for it, and they just rusted in the toolbox. I actually still have one of those wrenches. I use it sometimes when the radiator in my office acts up. It clanks so loudly in the winter, especially during my afternoon sessions. 

But, um... no, to answer your question, I haven't ever had a time where I felt depressed or down like this for weeks at a time. Just that stress in grad school, really.

doctor.intent: Determine if there have been any periods of elevated/expansive mood, increased goal-directed activity, or decreased need for sleep to rule out bipolar disorder and distinguish between major depressive disorder (single episode vs recurrent) and persistent depressive disorder
doctor.question: I want to ask about your energy and activity level more carefully. In these past 8 months, have there been any times—even just a few days—where you felt like you were doing MORE than usual, accomplishing more, or felt like you had more energy and drive, even if you wouldn't describe it as feeling 'good'?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of elevated energy, increased goal-directed activity, or manic/hypomanic symptoms. None of my symptom profile items (Delusions, Disorganized Abnormal Behavior, Negative Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration) cover manic or hypomanic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Um, more energy? No... no, I haven't had any days where I felt like I was doing more than usual. Honestly, getting out of bed has been the biggest accomplishment lately. 

I used to have so much energy, though. When I first started at the clinic, I was running two therapy groups a week on top of my individual caseload. We had this one group room, room B, and the chairs in there were those awful molded plastic ones from the nineties. They were this bright, obnoxious teal color. I tried for months to get the clinic director to approve a budget for new chairs. He was this very stern man who always drank his coffee out of a travel mug that looked like a camera lens. It was actually a really clever design, my nephew has one just like it. He's really into photography, mostly black and white landscapes. He took this incredible photo of a lone pine tree up in the mountains last winter. He printed it on this special textured paper and framed it for my birthday. I hung it right above the fireplace, but then the hook gave out a few weeks ago and it fell. Thankfully the glass didn't break, but it chipped the mantle... 

Sorry, I lost my train of thought. But no, I haven't felt any extra energy or drive or anything like that in the last eight months. Just... just the opposite, really.

doctor.intent: Determine if there's a pattern of recurrent depressive episodes (suggesting F33.9 Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent) versus a single episode (F32.9) or persistent depressive symptoms (F34.1 Persistent Depressive Disorder). The patient has denied prior depressive episodes, but I need to clarify whether there have been any mood changes in the year or two before these 8 months started.
doctor.question: In the year or two before these 8 months started—so roughly from two to three years ago until about 8 months ago—did you notice any periods where your mood felt lower, even if it wasn't as severe as what you're experiencing now?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of lower mood in the year or two before the current 8-month period, which is screening for prior depressive episodes or persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). This is not covered by the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um, in the year or two before all this started? No, I don't think so. I felt pretty normal back then. My mood was fine. 

That was around the time we finally decided to redo the kitchen, actually. We had these awful linoleum floors that were peeling up at the corners, and the cabinets were this really dark, depressing oak. We ended up going with a light gray for the cabinets, which really brightened the place up. The contractor we hired, his name was Dave, he was always bringing his golden retriever to the house while he worked. The dog's name was Buster, and he was the sweetest thing, but he shed everywhere. I was constantly vacuuming up dog hair, even after Dave left for the day. My husband bought one of those robot vacuums to help out, you know, the ones that just wander around the house on their own? It worked okay for a while, but then it got stuck under the sofa and just kept beeping until the battery died. I had to get down on my hands and knees with a broom handle to fish it out. It was covered in dust bunnies. I think we ended up giving it to my neighbor's daughter when she moved into her first apartment. She was so excited about it, she sent us a thank you card with a picture of her cat sitting on top of it...

But, wait. What were we talking about? Oh, my mood before all this. Yeah, no, I felt fine. I wasn't feeling low or anything like that. Just regular, you know?

inference.note: Ruled out F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder) - patient denies any prior depressive episodes of similar duration or severity. Ruled out F34.1 (dysthymia) - onset was acute 8 months ago, not lifelong pattern. Ruled out bipolar spectrum - patient explicitly denies any periods of elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, or increased goal-directed activity even when directly asked multiple times. Clear unipolar major depressive episode with 8-month duration, anhedonia, depressed mood, and no manic/hypomanic features.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a major depressive episode characterized by persistent depressed mood, anhedonia (loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities including social work, yoga, art galleries, journaling), and functional impairment lasting 8 months. No history of manic or hypomanic episodes. No prior episodes of depression lasting weeks or longer except for brief stress during graduate school. Symptoms are constant and pervasive without significant periods of improvement. The trigger appears to be a significant psychosocial stressor (taking in an older relative 8 months ago), which aligns with the onset timeline.
